title: Decommissioning projects in Germany and Switzerland near completion
html:
Since 20 November, the first steel plates have been cut out of Stade's spherical containment vessel using oxy-fuel cutting equipment. Previously, the outer concrete shell of the reactor building and the auxiliary buildings had been dismantled, and the exhaust stack demolished. The dismantling of the large steel sphere, from top to bottom, now marks the final visible step in the decommissioning of the site.

During the plant's operation, the containment vessel enclosed the reactor pressure vessel and essential parts of the primary cooling circuit. Now, the steel sphere is being dismantled downwards from its highest point at a height of about 48 metres.

Employees of contractor Freimuth are cutting individual plates from the steel shell from a work platform. The cut-out pieces of steel fall into the interior of the sphere, are subsequently retrieved, and further processed on another area of ​​the construction site. According to Freimuth, around 7,000 square metres of steel structure will be dismantled.

All remaining buildings and areas of the Stade site are to be dismantled by the end of 2027. The aim is to make the site available for future use.

"With the significant steel sphere measuring 48 metres in diameter, the Stade nuclear power plant now disappears from the horizon for good," said plant manager Marco Albers. "My thanks go to the team at Freimuth, who are carrying out this special task with great care and technical expertise."

Stade was the first power plant in Germany to be decommissioned after the country announced a nuclear phase-out policy in 2001. The 640 MWe pressurised water reactor began operating in 1972. The plant was shut down at end of 2005. Dismantling of the power plant began in October 2005. Conventional demolition of individual buildings on the power plant site started in 2023.

The first phase of the building dismantling was completed in spring 2024. It involved the demolition of 17 buildings with a total volume of about 177,000 cubic metres - including the administration building, the workshop and operations building, the emergency diesel generator building, the switchgear building, and finally the engine house. This work laid the foundation for the dismantling of the remaining central building complex. Aspects such as safety, environmental protection, and sustainability through material recycling were given top priority.


The containment vessel after most of the concrete had been removed (Image: Freimuth)

The demolition of the reactor building is part of Phase II of the conventional dismantling process and simultaneously marks the beginning of the crucial final phase of the overall project.

On 31 March this year, the demolition of the reactor building began. To weaken the material, a steel ball weighing about four tonnes was first used to strike the approximately 80-centimetre-thick concrete shell. Following this, the auxiliary buildings were completely demolished before the further demolition of the reactor building began at the beginning of June. This involved the use of, among other things, a 16-tonne hydraulic shear and a 180-tonne cable excavator.

Phases II (involving five building complexes) and III (ten building complexes) have been running in parallel since 2023. The site is scheduled to be released from nuclear regulatory oversight in autumn 2027. This will make the Stade nuclear power plant the first commercially operated pressurised water reactor in Germany to be completely dismantled.

Swiss research reactor

The Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) plans to demolish the concrete reactor building of the Saphir - Switzerland's first research reactor - in the coming months.


(Image: PSI)

The reactor had originally been built in 1955 at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the US state of Tennessee specifically for the first United Nations Atomic Energy Conference ('Atoms for Peace'). It was flown to Geneva, where it served as a demonstration reactor during the conference. The USA offered it for sale for USD250,000, including fuel, mechanics, and a control room. Switzerland decided to buy it.

The so-called swimming pool-type research reactor at Würenlingen, in the canton of Aargau, became operational in April 1957 at a power level of 1 MW. For 37 years it was the strongest neutron source within Switzerland for research purposes and industrial applications. The power level of 10 MW was reached in 1983 following the demands of the different facility users. Saphir remained in operation until the end of 1993.

In 1998, PSI submitted the decommissioning request to the Swiss nuclear regulator. The actual dismantling work began in 2002. By 2008, the reactor's internal components, its underwater installations, and the pool had largely been dismantled and removed.

Work to demolish the remaining concrete structure of the reactor is set to begin soon.

"Saphir is practically hollowed out inside," said plant manager Sophie Harzmann. What will be dismantled in the next three months is largely concrete. "And this was measured in elaborate measurement campaigns," she added. From this point on, the building can be demolished like a conventional building. "In about three months we will have a green meadow here again."

This is the first time in Switzerland that a former nuclear facility, including its building, has been completely removed.

In parallel with the Saphir project, work is also under way at PSI to dismantle the former Diorit research reactor. The experimental incineration plant - where low-level radioactive waste was once incinerated - is also slated for demolition. "For us, Saphir is also a pilot project," Harzmann said. "We want to use the experience we've gained here for future dismantling projects." This knowledge will be particularly important at Diorit. The facility is larger and more complex than Saphir and presents the team with new challenges.

During the dismantling process, PSI also regularly exchanges information with other nuclear facility operators, including the Mühleberg nuclear power plant - a single 373 MWe boiling water reactor that began operations in 1972 and was shut down in December 2019. "Every facility is unique, but there are many common challenges that shouldn't have to be solved by each operator alone," said Sabine Mayer, head of Radiation Safety and Security at PSI. "By sharing experiences and solutions, we can learn from each other."
summary: The dismantling of the steel sphere of the containment vessel has begun at the decommissioned Stade nuclear power plant in Germany. Meanwhile, the demolition of the remaining concrete structure of Switzerland's Saphir research reactor is set to start.
